intro: The story of Babel is short, only nine verses in Genesis 11. People build a tower. Their language gets mixed up, and they are scattered. Right before it, Genesis 10 lists about seventy nations. Right after it, God calls one man, Abram. This unit reads these chapters together, beside other old texts.

You will read old copies of Deuteronomy 32:8 from the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Greek Septuagint. You will meet old Jewish books, like Jubilees, Sirach and the history of Josephus. You will also meet modern scholars, like Mark S. Smith and Michael Heiser. They do not all agree, and you will see why.

By the end, you will be able to retell the Babel story and compare old copies of Deuteronomy 32:8. You will describe how different readers explain the gods of the nations. You will also trace the promise to Abram, that all families of the earth would be blessed, and explain how Jewish and Christian readers understand it.
bigQuestion: What happened to the nations after Babel, and how did the promise to Abram speak to them, as ancient and modern readers see it?

write.prompt: Did God give up on the nations after Babel? Use at least two passages from this unit, such as Genesis 11:1–9, Deuteronomy 32:8–9, Sirach 17:17, Genesis 12:1–3 or Psalm 82:8. Tell what each passage says. Then explain how two readers understood it, such as Rashi, Jubilees, Mark Smith or Michael Heiser.

title: Babel and the Nations

chapters.title: The Tower and the Gods of the Nations
chapters.bigQuestion: What does the Bible say happened to the nations after Babel, and how have readers explained it?

story.title: Seventy Names on a Map
story.kicker: Maya counts the nations in Genesis 10 and finds a number that shows up again and again.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz unrolled a big paper map across two desks. It showed the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. It stretched east to the rivers of Iraq. "This is the world the writers of Genesis knew," she said. "Today we will read a list of nations." Maya held a pencil and a stack of sticky notes.

The class opened to Genesis 10. The chapter lists the families that came from Noah's three sons, Shem, Ham and Japheth. Each time Maya read a new name, she wrote it on a note. She stuck it on the map. Some names were easy, like Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt. Others, like Tarshish, made the class guess and look things up.

When the list ended, Maya counted her notes. "Seventy!" she said. Ms. Ortiz smiled. "Many readers count seventy in the Hebrew text," she said. "The old Greek translation has a couple more. That number, seventy, shows up in some surprising places."

"Where else?" asked Maya. Ms. Ortiz pointed to the next chapter, Genesis 11, and the tower of Babel. Then she held up the book of Deuteronomy. "Many scholars read these chapters together," she said. "Old copies of Deuteronomy may tell us who was put in charge of the nations. Let's read them and see."
story.think: Why do you think Genesis puts a long list of nations right before the story of the tower of Babel?

lessons.title: One Language, One Plan
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 11 says everyone spoke one language and decided to build a city and a tower that reached toward the sky.
reading: Genesis 11 begins with a picture. The whole earth had one language. People moved east and settled on a plain in the land of *Shinar*. There they made bricks and baked them hard. They used a sticky black tar to hold the bricks together.

Shinar is an old name for southern *Mesopotamia*. That is the land between two great rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. Today most of it is in Iraq. In the story, the people made a plan there. They would build a city and a tower whose top reached into the sky (Genesis 11:4).

The builders gave two reasons. They wanted to make a name for themselves. They also did not want to be scattered over the earth. Earlier, God had told Noah's family to fill the earth (Genesis 9:1). Many Jewish and Christian readers see Babel as a story about pride. The builders put their own name first.

words.d: an old name for southern Mesopotamia, where the story of Babel takes place
the land between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, mostly in today's Iraq

look.title: Genesis 11:4 in Simple Words
look.text: The people said to each other: Come, let us build a city and a tower that reaches up to the sky. Then we will be famous, and we will not be scattered all over the earth.
look.cite: Genesis 11:4, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: What two things did the builders want? Which one goes against God's words to Noah in Genesis 9:1?

check.q: Where did the builders settle, according to Genesis 11?
choices: On a plain in the land of Shinar
On an island in the sea
check.why: Genesis 11:2 says the people settled on a plain in Shinar, an old name for southern Mesopotamia.

check.q: What did the builders want for themselves?
choices: To spread out over the whole earth
To make a name for themselves
To build a boat for the animals
check.why: Genesis 11:4 says the builders wanted to make a name for themselves and stay together.

check.q: Why do many readers see Babel as a story about pride?
choices: The builders were too tired to finish
The builders wanted to be famous and stay in one place
The builders wanted to leave the city
The builders asked God for help
check.why: The builders put their own name first and did not want to fill the earth, as God had told Noah's family in Genesis 9:1.

lessons.title: God Comes Down
lessons.mainIdea: In the story, God comes down, mixes up the people's language and scatters them, and the city is called Babel.
reading: Genesis 11:5 says the LORD came down to see the city and the tower. The builders wanted to reach up to heaven. Instead, God comes down to them. Many readers notice the gentle joke here. The tower seemed very tall to its builders. Yet God still had to come down to see it.

Then God speaks. In Genesis 11:7, God says, let us go down and mix up their language. Who is us? Philo, a Jewish writer in Egypt, wrote a whole book on this story. It is called On the Confusion of Tongues. He said God was speaking with the heavenly powers that serve him. Many scholars today say God is speaking to his *divine council*.

Other readers hear a royal way of speaking, like a king who says we. Some Christians hear a hint of the Trinity. After God speaks, the people cannot understand each other. They stop building and spread out. The city is named *Babel*. It sounds like balal, a Hebrew word that means to mix up. Babel is also the Hebrew name for Babylon.

words.d: God's heavenly court: the spirit beings around God's throne, as in Psalm 82
the city in Genesis 11; its name sounds like the Hebrew word for mix up, and it is the Hebrew name for Babylon

look.title: Two Readings of Let Us
look.text: Genesis 11:7: God says, Let us go down and mix up their language. Reading A (Philo long ago, and many scholars today): God is speaking to heavenly beings around him, like a king speaking to his court. Reading B (some other readers): God is speaking in a royal way, the way a king might say we. Many Christians also hear a hint of the Trinity.
look.prompt: Which clue in the verse would each reader point to? Could another verse with us, like Genesis 1:26, help you think about it?

check.q: According to Genesis 11:5, what did the LORD do?
choices: Came down to see the city and the tower
check.why: Genesis 11:5 says the LORD came down to see the city and the tower the people were building.

check.q: Who did Philo say God was speaking with when he said let us?
choices: The heavenly powers that serve him
check.why: In On the Confusion of Tongues, Philo explained let us as God speaking with the heavenly powers that serve him.

check.q: The name Babel sounds like a Hebrew word that means what?
check.why: Babel sounds like balal, the Hebrew word for mix up, which is what happened to the people's language.

lessons.title: A Tower Like a Ziggurat
lessons.mainIdea: The tower was likely pictured as a ziggurat, and readers from Josephus to Heiser have asked what the builders wanted.
reading: Archaeologists have found the remains of ziggurats in Iraq. A *ziggurat* was a tall tower built in steps, like a giant staircase. It stood beside a temple. People in Mesopotamia believed a god could come down to the temple there. The great ziggurat of Babylon was called Etemenanki. Its name means temple of the foundation of heaven and earth.

Many scholars think the tower of Babel was pictured as a ziggurat. The Jewish historian Josephus retold the story around 94 CE, in his Antiquities of the Jews. He said a proud king named Nimrod led the builders. He said they used baked brick and tar, as Genesis does. Genesis itself never names a leader for the tower.

Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Bible's old languages, thought the builders wanted to bring the gods down on their own terms. In The Unseen Realm (2015), he called Babel the third big *rebellion* in Genesis, after Eden and Genesis 6. Other readers agree Babel is about pride. They may not count it as one of three.

words.d: a tall tower built in steps beside a temple in ancient Mesopotamia
a turning against the one in charge; refusing to follow

look.title: Picture a Ziggurat
look.text: Picture a hill made of dried mud bricks, flat on top, rising in wide steps. Each step is smaller than the one below. A long staircase climbs the front. At the very top stands a small shrine. The people below believed their god could come down to this place.
look.prompt: Why might a tower like this remind readers of the tower of Babel, whose top reached toward the sky?

check.q: What was a ziggurat?
choices: A tall stepped tower beside a temple
check.why: A ziggurat was a tall tower built in steps beside a temple in Mesopotamia.

check.q: Heiser called Babel the third rebellion. Which were the first two?
choices: The Exodus and the golden calf
Cain and Abel, and Noah's ark
The call of Abram and the flood
Eden and the sons of God in Genesis 6
check.why: In Heiser's reading, Eden was the first rebellion, Genesis 6 the second, and Babel the third.

check.q: Who did Josephus say led the builders of the tower?
check.why: In his Antiquities of the Jews, Josephus said Nimrod led the builders. Genesis 11 itself does not name a leader.

lessons.title: Noah's Three Sons
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 10 lists the peoples who came from Noah's sons Shem, Ham and Japheth, and scholars call it the Table of Nations.
reading: Genesis 10 is a long list of names. It is often called the *Table of Nations*. It tells which peoples came from each of Noah's three sons: Japheth, Ham and Shem. Many names are people. Many are also names of lands or cities. The list moves from one son to the next.

Each part of the list ends the same way. It says these peoples had their own families, languages, lands and *nations* (Genesis 10:5, 20 and 31). Some names are easy to know. Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt. Canaan is the land where Israel later lived. Other names, like Tarshish, still puzzle scholars.

The list also names Nimrod, a mighty hunter and king. Genesis 10:10 says his kingdom began in Babel and other cities in Shinar. So Genesis 10 mentions Babel before chapter 11 tells its story. The two chapters are linked. Chapter 10 shows the nations spread out. Chapter 11 then tells a story about why.

words.d: the name scholars give to the list of peoples in Genesis 10
large groups of people who share a land, a language or a family story

look.title: Genesis 10:32 in Simple Words
look.text: These are the families of Noah's sons, listed by their family lines and their nations. From them the nations were divided and spread out over the earth after the flood.
look.cite: Genesis 10:32, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: This verse closes the list. Which words in it point ahead to the story of Babel in Genesis 11?

check.q: What do scholars call the list of peoples in Genesis 10?
check.why: Genesis 10 is called the Table of Nations because it lists the peoples who came from Noah's sons.

check.q: Which name in Genesis 10 is the Hebrew name for Egypt?
check.why: Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt. Shinar is southern Mesopotamia, and Tarshish is still debated.

check.q: Why is Nimrod in Genesis 10 a link to Genesis 11?
choices: He was the father of Abram
check.why: Genesis 10:10 says Nimrod's kingdom began in Babel, the city whose story comes in Genesis 11.

lessons.title: Counting Seventy
lessons.mainIdea: Readers count about seventy nations in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10, and seventy came to stand for all the nations.
reading: Readers who count the names in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10 get about seventy. The *Septuagint* has a couple more, about seventy-two. The Septuagint is an old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible. Its first books were made in Egypt around 250 BCE. In later Jewish writing, the seventy nations came to mean all the peoples of the world.

The number seventy shows up in Israel's own story too. Genesis 46:27 and Exodus 1:5 say seventy people from Jacob's family went down to Egypt. So the world has seventy nations, and Israel begins with seventy people. Many readers think this match is on purpose.

Clay tablets from *Ugarit*, an old city in Syria, add another seventy. They tell of the high god El and his wife Athirat, who had seventy sons. E. Theodore Mullen studied El's council in these tablets in a 1980 book. Mark S. Smith (2001) and other scholars compare this picture with Deuteronomy 32, later in this chapter.

words.d: an old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in Egypt around 250 BCE
an ancient city in Syria whose clay tablets tell stories of the god El and his council

look.title: Nations in Genesis 10, by Son of Noah
look.cite: Genesis 10, Hebrew (Masoretic) text; a common scholarly count
look.prompt: Add the three numbers. What total do you get? Why do readers care about that number?

check.q: About how many nations do readers count in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10?
check.why: The usual count of nations in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10 is seventy: 14 from Japheth, 30 from Ham and 26 from Shem.

check.q: What is the Septuagint?
choices: An old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible
check.why: The Septuagint is the old Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, begun in Egypt around 250 BCE.

check.q: What do clay tablets from Ugarit say about the high god El?
choices: He and his wife had seventy sons
check.why: The Ugarit tablets tell of El and his wife Athirat, who had seventy sons. Scholars such as Mark S. Smith compare this to the seventy nations.

lessons.title: First the List, Then the Story
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis puts the list of nations before the Babel story, so readers see the result first and then the story of why.
reading: Genesis 10 comes before Genesis 11, but the events are not in that order. Genesis 10 already shows many languages. Genesis 11 begins with one language. So the writer shows the result first. Then he goes back to tell the story behind it. Storytellers still do this today.

Genesis 10:25 gives a clue. It names a man called *Peleg*. It says that in his days the earth was divided. The name Peleg sounds like the Hebrew word for divide. Many readers link this verse to the scattering at Babel. Others think it means something else, such as a dividing of land.

Deuteronomy 32:8 also talks about God dividing the nations. Many scholars read Genesis 10, Genesis 11 and this verse together. In that reading, the three passages tell one story. People were scattered at Babel. Then God did something about the nations. The next section reads what Deuteronomy says he did.

words.d: a man in Genesis 10:25 whose name sounds like the Hebrew word for divide
to spread out in many directions; in Genesis 11 the builders are scattered over the earth

look.title: Result First, Story Second
look.text: Imagine a picture book. The first page shows a broken vase on the floor. The next page goes back in time. It shows the cat jumping on the shelf. Genesis 10 is like the first page: the nations are already spread out. Genesis 11 is like the next page: it tells how it happened.
look.prompt: Why might a writer show the result first and tell the story second? Can you think of a book or movie that does this?

check.q: Which detail shows that Genesis 11 goes back in time from Genesis 10?
choices: It begins with the whole earth speaking one language
It tells of Abram leaving Haran
check.why: Genesis 10 already shows many languages, but Genesis 11 begins with one language, so it goes back to tell how the change happened.

check.q: What does the name Peleg sound like in Hebrew?
check.why: Genesis 10:25 says the earth was divided in Peleg's days, and his name sounds like the Hebrew word for divide.

check.q: Which later verse also speaks of God dividing the nations?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32:8 speaks of the Most High dividing the nations, so many scholars read it with Genesis 10 and 11.

sections.title: Moses' Song and the Old Copies

lessons.title: The Most High Divides the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 32:8–9 says the Most High divided the nations and set their borders, and the LORD kept Israel as his portion.
reading: Deuteronomy 32 is a long poem. It is often called the Song of Moses. In the story, Moses teaches it to Israel near the end of his life. The song looks back over Israel's history. Verse 8 looks all the way back to the time the nations were split up.

Verse 8 says the *Most High* gave the nations their *inheritance*. He divided the peoples and set their borders. Verse 9 says the LORD's *portion* is his people. Jacob, another name for Israel, is his share. So the nations get their lands. The LORD keeps one people for himself.

One phrase in verse 8 is hard. It says the borders were set by the number of someone. But whose number? Old copies of the Bible say different things here. Scholars have written a great deal about this small phrase. The next lesson shows the choices.

words.d: a title for God in the Hebrew Bible, meaning the highest one over all
land or goods given to someone to keep, often passed down in a family
a share that belongs to someone; Deuteronomy 32:9 calls Israel the LORD's portion

look.title: Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in Simple Words
look.text: When the Most High gave the nations their lands, when he split up the families of people, he set their borders by the number of ______. But the LORD's own share is his people. Jacob is the part he chose for himself.
look.cite: Deuteronomy 32:8–9, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611); the blank marks the words old copies disagree on
look.prompt: The blank is the puzzle of this section. Before you read on, what words do you think might fit there?

check.q: What is Deuteronomy 32 often called?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32 is a poem that Moses teaches Israel, so it is often called the Song of Moses.

check.q: What does Deuteronomy 32:9 call the LORD's portion?
check.why: Deuteronomy 32:9 says the LORD's portion is his people, and Jacob is his share.

check.q: What does the title Most High mean?
check.why: Most High is a title for God in the Hebrew Bible. It means the highest one over all.

lessons.title: Sons of Israel or Sons of God?
lessons.mainIdea: The standard Hebrew text says sons of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:8, but a Dead Sea Scroll says sons of God, and the Septuagint points the same way.
reading: Most printed Hebrew Bibles use the *Masoretic Text*. Careful Jewish scribes called the Masoretes copied it. Its oldest complete copy of the Hebrew Bible, the Leningrad Codex, was made in 1008 CE. In Deuteronomy 32:8, this text says the borders were set by the number of the sons of Israel. The King James Version follows it.

In 1947, people began finding the *Dead Sea Scrolls* in caves near the Dead Sea. Many of the scrolls are more than two thousand years old. One copy of Deuteronomy from these caves says sons of God in verse 8. Many copies of the Greek Septuagint point the same way. They say angels of God or sons of God.

So which reading came first? Many scholars, such as Mark S. Smith, think sons of God is older. They think a later scribe changed it, perhaps to avoid talk of other heavenly beings. Scholars who disagree on much else agree on this. Some newer English Bibles now follow the scroll. Others keep sons of Israel and add a note.

words.d: the standard Hebrew text of the Bible, carefully copied by Jewish scribes called the Masoretes
very old scrolls found in caves near the Dead Sea starting in 1947, including copies of Bible books
a person whose job was to copy writings by hand

look.title: How Old Are the Witnesses?
rows: Septuagint of the Torah first made (c. 250 BCE)
Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy (c. 50 BCE)
look.cite: Common scholarly dates for the Septuagint, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Leningrad Codex
look.prompt: Which witness is oldest? Why might scholars pay close attention to an older copy?

check.q: What does the Masoretic Text say in Deuteronomy 32:8?
check.why: The Masoretic Text, and the King James Version that follows it, say sons of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:8.

check.q: Where were the Dead Sea Scrolls found?
choices: In caves near the Dead Sea
check.why: The Dead Sea Scrolls were found in caves near the Dead Sea, beginning in 1947.

check.q: Which reading of Deuteronomy 32:8 do many scholars now think is older?
choices: Sons of God, as in the Dead Sea Scroll
Sons of Israel, as in the Leningrad Codex
check.why: Many scholars think sons of God, the reading of a Dead Sea Scroll, is older, and that a later scribe changed it.

lessons.title: Rulers Over the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Old Jewish books like Sirach and Jubilees say God set rulers over the nations, and Heiser read Deuteronomy 32 the same way.
reading: Other old Jewish books also say the nations were given heavenly rulers. Sirach was written around 180 BCE. It says God set a ruler over every nation, but Israel is the Lord's portion (Sirach 17:17). The book of *Jubilees* says God put spirits in charge of the nations. But over Israel, it says, God alone rules (Jubilees 15:31–32).

Many scholars follow sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8 and read it this way too. Michael Heiser built a large idea on it. In his reading, after Babel God set the nations under the sons of God, lesser *elohim* in his council. God kept one people for himself, Israel. That is why verse 9 calls Israel his portion.

Elohim is a Hebrew word. It can mean God. It can also mean other spirit beings. Psalm 82 shows God judging the elohim for being unfair to the weak. Heiser read the gods of the nations as spirit beings that became *corrupt*, not only statues. He argued that the LORD made them and is far above them.

words.d: an old Jewish book, written around 150 BCE, that retells the stories of Genesis and early Exodus
a Hebrew word that can mean God, gods, or other spirit beings
turned bad; no longer doing what is right

look.title: Sirach 17:17 in Simple Words
look.text: When God divided the nations of the whole earth, he set a ruler over every people. But Israel is the Lord's own portion.
look.cite: Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 17:17, paraphrased from the King James Version Apocrypha (1611)
look.prompt: Which words here sound like Deuteronomy 32:8–9? What does Sirach add?

check.q: In Heiser's reading, who did God put over the nations after Babel?
choices: Lesser elohim, the sons of God
check.why: Heiser read Deuteronomy 32:8 to say God set the nations under the sons of God, lesser elohim in his council.

check.q: What can the Hebrew word elohim mean?
check.why: Elohim can mean God, and it can also name other spirit beings, as in Psalm 82.

check.q: Which old book says God set a ruler over every nation, but Israel is the Lord's portion?
check.why: Sirach 17:17 says God set a ruler over every people, but Israel is the Lord's portion.

lessons.title: Other Ways to Read It
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 4:19–20 shows a similar pattern, and readers explain the sons in Deuteronomy 32:8 in different ways.
reading: Deuteronomy 4:19–20 has a similar pattern. There Moses warns Israel not to worship the sun, moon and stars, the *host of heaven*. He says the LORD gave these to all the nations. But the LORD took Israel out of Egypt to be his own people. Many readers see the same idea as in Deuteronomy 32.

Not everyone reads it this way. Rashi was a famous Jewish teacher in France who died in 1105. He followed sons of Israel. He linked the seventy nations to the seventy people of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt. Many Christian readers have also kept sons of Israel.

Other Jewish and Christian readers follow sons of God, or the Septuagint's angels of God, but read them as *guardian angels*. In this view, each nation has an angel who watches over it. Daniel 10:20 speaks of a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece. All these readers agree the verse is about God and the nations.

words.d: the sun, moon and stars; in some verses, also the heavenly beings around God
angels that some readers believe watch over a person or a nation

look.title: Three Readings Side by Side
look.text: Deuteronomy 32:8, by the number of ______. Reading 1 (Masoretic Text, Rashi): sons of Israel, like the seventy of Jacob's family. Reading 2 (Heiser and some others): sons of God, lesser elohim who ruled the nations and became corrupt. Reading 3 (many early readers): angels of God who guard the nations.
look.prompt: What do all three readings agree on? Where do they differ?

check.q: In Deuteronomy 4:19, what does Moses warn Israel not to worship?
check.why: Deuteronomy 4:19 warns against worshiping the sun, moon and stars, the host of heaven.

check.q: How did Rashi explain sons of Israel in Deuteronomy 32:8?
choices: As the angels of the nations
As the seventy of Jacob's family who went to Egypt
check.why: Rashi linked the seventy nations to the seventy people of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt.

check.q: What does Daniel 10:20 mention?
choices: A prince of Persia and a prince of Greece
check.why: Daniel 10:20 speaks of a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece, which some readers take as angels over nations.

review.q: In Genesis 11, what did the builders want to build?
choices: A city and a tower reaching toward the sky
review.why: Genesis 11:4 says the people planned a city and a tower whose top reached into the sky.

review.q: Which ancient Jewish writer wrote a book about Babel called On the Confusion of Tongues?
review.why: Philo of Alexandria wrote On the Confusion of Tongues about the Babel story. Josephus retold it in his Antiquities.
Genesis 10 lists the peoples who came from Noah's sons, so it is called the Table of Nations.

review.q: Why is the number seventy important in this chapter?
choices: It is the number of bricks in the tower
It is Noah's age at the flood
It is the usual count of nations in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10
It is the number of psalms
review.why: Readers count seventy nations in the Hebrew text of Genesis 10, and seventy came to stand for all nations.

review.q: Which old copy says sons of God in Deuteronomy 32:8?
choices: A Dead Sea Scroll of Deuteronomy
review.why: A Dead Sea Scroll copy of Deuteronomy says sons of God. The Masoretic Text and the King James say sons of Israel.

review.q: What does Deuteronomy 32:9 say is the LORD's portion?
review.why: Deuteronomy 32:9 says the LORD's portion is his people, Jacob.

review.q: Which reader followed sons of Israel and linked it to Jacob's family of seventy?
review.why: Rashi, a Jewish teacher in France, linked the verse to the seventy of Jacob's family who went to Egypt.

review.q: How is Heiser's reading different from the guardian angel reading?
choices: Heiser saw the sons of God as lesser elohim who became corrupt rulers
Heiser said there were no nations
Heiser said Babel did not matter
review.why: Both readings follow sons of God, but Heiser saw them as lesser elohim who ruled the nations badly, as in Psalm 82.

chapters.title: Abraham and God's Own Portion
chapters.bigQuestion: Why does the Bible tell Abram's story right after Babel, and what did the promise to bless all nations mean to its readers?

story.title: Packing Up in Haran
story.kicker: A servant boy asks Abram where the family is going, and the answer surprises him.
paragraphs: The tents in Haran were coming down. Camels knelt while servants tied on water skins and rolled up rugs. Sheep and goats called out in the dust. Abram, who was seventy-five years old, walked among them. His wife Sarai counted jars of grain. His nephew Lot checked the ropes on the donkeys.

A young servant boy lifted a basket, then set it down again. "Master Abram," he asked, "where are we going?" Abram looked out past the fields. "To a land God will show me," he said. The boy frowned. "But you do not know where it is?" Abram smiled. "Not yet."

The Bible tells this moment in just a few verses, in Genesis 12. In the story, God tells Abram to leave his country, his relatives and his father's house. God promises to make him a great nation and to bless him. Then comes the biggest promise. Through Abram, all the families of the earth will be blessed.

This story comes right after Babel, where the nations were scattered. Many readers notice that timing, and they think it matters. The nations had just been sent away. Now God was starting a new family. The promise said this one family would bring blessing to all the others.
story.think: Why might it matter that God's call to Abram comes right after the story of Babel?

lessons.title: From Ur to Haran
lessons.mainIdea: Abram's family came from Ur and settled in Haran, and Joshua 24:2 says his father's family served other gods.
reading: At the end of Genesis 11, the story narrows to one family. Terah had three sons: Abram, Nahor and Haran. Abram married Sarai. Genesis 11:30 says Sarai had no children. Terah took Abram, Sarai and his grandson Lot and left *Ur*. They set out for Canaan. But they stopped in the city of *Haran* and settled there.

Ur was a great city in southern Mesopotamia. Archaeologists have dug up its ziggurat, and part of it still stands. Haran was a trading town far to the north, in what is now Turkey. Both cities honored the moon god. In Ur he was called Nanna. In Haran he was called Sin.

Joshua 24:2 adds a detail. It says Abram's ancestors, including Terah, lived beyond the river and served other gods. So Abram did not come from a family that already followed Israel's God. Later Jewish writers told more. The book of *Jubilees* (chapter 12) says young Abram turned from idols and prayed to the one God.

words.d: an ancient city in southern Mesopotamia; Genesis 11 says Abram's family came from there
an ancient trading town in what is now Turkey, where Abram's family settled; also the name of Abram's brother
an old Jewish book, written around 150 BCE, that retells the stories of Genesis and early Exodus

look.title: Trace the Journey
look.text: Picture a map. Put one finger on Ur, near where the Euphrates River meets the sea. Slide it north and west along the river, a very long way, to Haran. Then turn south, down into the land of Canaan, near the Mediterranean Sea. That is the path the story gives for Abram's family.
look.prompt: Why do you think the journey took the family north first instead of straight west across the desert?

check.q: Which city did Terah's family leave first?
check.why: Genesis 11:31 says Terah's family left Ur and settled in Haran on the way to Canaan.

check.q: What does Joshua 24:2 say about Abram's ancestors?
choices: They wrote the Table of Nations
They built the tower of Babel
check.why: Joshua 24:2 says Abram's ancestors, including Terah, served other gods.

check.q: Which god did both Ur and Haran honor?
check.why: Both cities honored the moon god, called Nanna in Ur and Sin in Haran.

lessons.title: Go to the Land
lessons.mainIdea: In Genesis 12:1–7, God tells Abram to leave his land and family, and Abram goes at age seventy-five into Canaan.
reading: Genesis 12:1 begins with a command. God tells Abram to go. He must leave three things: his country, his relatives and his father's house. Each one is closer to home than the last. God does not name the new land. He says only that he will show it to Abram.

Genesis 12:4 says Abram went, as the LORD had told him. He was seventy-five years old. Sarai and Lot went too, with the people and goods they had gained in Haran. They traveled into Canaan. At Shechem, God promised this land to Abram's *offspring* (Genesis 12:7). Abram built an *altar* there.

The New Testament book of Hebrews looks back on this moment. Hebrews 11:8 says Abraham went out without knowing where he was going. Jewish and Christian readers both honor Abraham's trust. A Jewish teaching in Pirkei Avot 5:3 says Abraham was tested ten times. Jewish tradition counts this journey among the tests.

words.d: a person's children, grandchildren and all who come after them
a raised place, often of stones, where people offered gifts and worship to God

look.title: Abram's Age in Genesis
look.prompt: How many years pass in the story between Abram leaving Haran and the birth of Isaac?

check.q: What three things did God tell Abram to leave in Genesis 12:1?
choices: His tent, his camels and his sheep
His city, his temple and his king
His country, his relatives and his father's house
His tower, his bricks and his tar
check.why: Genesis 12:1 names his country, his relatives and his father's house, each closer to home than the last.

check.q: How old was Abram when he left Haran?
check.why: Genesis 12:4 says Abram was seventy-five years old when he left Haran.

check.q: What does Hebrews 11:8 say about Abraham's journey?
choices: He went out not knowing where he was going
check.why: Hebrews 11:8 says Abraham went out without knowing where he was going.

lessons.title: A Great Name
lessons.mainIdea: At Babel people tried to make a name for themselves, but in Genesis 12:2 God promises to make Abram's name great.
reading: Put Genesis 11:4 and Genesis 12:2 side by side. At Babel, the builders wanted to make a name for themselves. Just one chapter later, God tells Abram, I will make your name great. The same Hebrew word for name, *shem*, is in both verses. Shem is also the name of Noah's son, Abram's ancestor.

Many Jewish and Christian readers notice this match. The builders reached for a great name by their own work. Abram receives a great name as a *promise*. The builders tried to stay together in one place. Abram leaves home and trusts what God said. The two stories seem to answer each other.

In the story, God does not destroy the scattered nations. Instead he starts over with one man and his family. Many readers see Abram's call as the turning point after Babel. The builders tried to hold on to one place. Abram lets go of his home. Through his family, the promise says, blessing will reach the nations again.

words.d: the Hebrew word for name; also the name of Noah's son, Abram's ancestor
words that say someone will surely do something

look.title: Two Verses Side by Side
look.text: Genesis 11:4: The builders say, Let us make a name for ourselves. Genesis 12:2: God says to Abram, I will make your name great. In both verses the Hebrew word for name is shem.
look.prompt: Who makes the name in each verse? What difference does that make in each story?

check.q: What is the Hebrew word for name?
check.why: Shem is the Hebrew word for name. It appears in both Genesis 11:4 and Genesis 12:2.

check.q: In Genesis 12:2, who promises to make Abram's name great?
check.why: In Genesis 12:2, God is the one who promises to make Abram's name great.

check.q: How are the builders of Babel and Abram different?
choices: The builders tried to make their own name; Abram was promised a great name
The builders left home; Abram stayed
check.why: At Babel the builders reached for a name by their own work. In Genesis 12:2, Abram receives a great name as a promise.

lessons.title: The Promises to Abram
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 12:2–3 gives a set of promises: a great nation, blessing, a great name, and blessing for all the families of the earth.
reading: Genesis 12:2–3 is short, but it is packed with promises. God says he will make Abram a great nation. He will bless Abram. He will make his name great. Abram will be a *blessing* to others. These first promises are about Abram's own family growing and doing well.

Then the promises reach outward. God says he will bless those who bless Abram. He will *curse* whoever treats Abram with scorn. Then comes the last promise. In Abram, all the families of the earth will be blessed. Many readers see this last line as the biggest of all.

At that moment Abram and Sarai had no children at all. So the promise of a great nation sounds almost impossible. That is part of the story's pull. Readers wait through many chapters to see what happens. Genesis 21 finally tells of the birth of their son, Isaac.

words.d: a gift of good things, or words that wish someone good
words that call for harm; the opposite of a blessing

look.title: Genesis 12:2–3 in Simple Words
look.text: I will make you into a great nation. I will bless you and make your name great, and you will be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, and curse those who curse you. Through you, all the families of the earth will be blessed.
look.cite: Genesis 12:2–3, paraphrased from the King James Version (1611)
look.prompt: Find the promises that are about Abram. Then find the one about everyone else. Why might readers call that one the biggest?

check.q: What is the last promise in Genesis 12:3?
choices: Abram would become king of Babylon
All the families of the earth would be blessed through him
Abram would go back to Ur
check.why: Genesis 12:3 ends with the promise that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abram.

check.q: Why does the promise of a great nation sound surprising?
choices: Abram and Sarai had no children yet
check.why: Genesis 11:30 says Sarai had no children, so a great nation from Abram sounds almost impossible.

check.q: Which chapter of Genesis tells of Isaac's birth?
check.why: Genesis 21 tells of the birth of Isaac to Abraham and Sarah.

lessons.title: All the Families of the Earth
lessons.mainIdea: The promise to bless all families points back to the scattered nations of Genesis 10 and forward through the rest of Genesis.
reading: Genesis 10 listed the families of the earth, spread out by their languages and lands. Genesis 12:3 uses the same Hebrew word for families, *mishpachah*. So the promise points back to that list. In the story, the scattered nations are not forgotten. The blessing is meant to reach them.

Genesis repeats the promise later. In Genesis 22:18, God tells Abraham that all the nations of the earth will be blessed through his offspring. In Genesis 26:4, the promise is repeated to Isaac. In Genesis 28:14, it is repeated to Jacob. Three *generations* hear the same promise.

Genesis is shaped around this turn. Chapters 1 to 11 tell about the whole world. Chapters 12 to 50 follow one family. Some readers compare it to a camera zooming in. The story narrows to Abraham's family, but the promise keeps the whole world in view.

words.d: the Hebrew word for a family or clan, used in Genesis 10 and in Genesis 12:3
the steps in a family line: parents, then children, then grandchildren

look.title: How Genesis Is Divided
look.cite: Genesis 1–50; a common way to divide the book
look.prompt: How many chapters are about the whole world? How many follow Abraham's family in all?

check.q: Which Hebrew word for families is used in both Genesis 10 and Genesis 12:3?
check.why: Mishpachah, the word for a family or clan, is used in the Table of Nations and in the promise of Genesis 12:3.

check.q: In Genesis 28:14, to whom is the promise repeated?
check.why: Genesis 28:14 repeats the promise to Jacob, Abraham's grandson.

check.q: About how many chapters of Genesis follow Abraham's family?
check.why: Genesis 12 to 50 follows Abraham's family. That is thirty-nine chapters.

lessons.title: A New Family After Babel
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis puts Abram's call right after Babel, and Heiser argued God began a new family to win back the nations.
reading: Look at the order of Genesis. Chapter 10 lists the nations. Chapter 11 scatters them at Babel. Chapter 12 begins with God calling Abram. Michael Heiser read this order with Deuteronomy 32:8–9 in mind. In his reading, God set the nations under *lesser elohim*. Then, right away, he called Abram. God gave up the nations for a time, but not for good.

Heiser often spoke of God's family. In his reading, God wanted a family in heaven, the sons of God, and a family on earth, people. Eden had held both together. After Babel, Abram's line would be the start of the earthly family again. Through it, the blessing would one day reach every nation.

So, for Heiser, Abram's call began a long plan to *reclaim* the nations. Israel was to be the family through whom they would be won back. Other readers put more weight on Abram's faith and God's covenant with his family. Many readers see both themes in the text.

words.d: Heiser's phrase for the spirit beings God set over the nations; lower than God, who made them
to take back something that was yours

look.title: Heiser's Idea in Plain Words
look.text: Right after Babel, God called Abram. The nations had been set under other gods. With Abram, God began a new family. Through that family he meant to win the nations back.
look.cite: Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm (Lexham Press, 2015); his idea described in our own words, not quoted
look.prompt: What two stories did Heiser connect here? How does the order of Genesis 11 and 12 help his idea?

check.q: According to Heiser, why does it matter that Abram's call comes right after Babel?
choices: Because God starts a new family right after giving the nations to others
check.why: Heiser thought the order was the point: God set the nations under lesser elohim, then began a new family with Abram.

check.q: What two families did Heiser say God wanted?
choices: A family in heaven and a family on earth
A family in Ur and a family in Haran
A family of kings and a family of priests
A family of giants and a family of angels
check.why: Heiser described God as wanting a family in heaven, the sons of God, and a family on earth, people.

check.q: What do some other readers put more weight on in Genesis 12?
choices: Abram's faith and God's covenant with his family
check.why: Other readers stress Abram's faith and God's covenant with his family, and many see both themes in Genesis 12.

lessons.title: Israel, the LORD's Portion
lessons.mainIdea: Deuteronomy 32:9 calls Israel the LORD's portion, and Exodus 19:5–6 calls Israel a treasured people and a kingdom of priests.
reading: Deuteronomy 32:9 says the LORD's portion is his people. Jacob is his share. A portion is a share, like a piece of land given to a family. In this verse, the nations get their lands, but the LORD keeps a people. The people of Israel come from Abram's grandson Jacob, who was also called Israel.

Exodus 19:5–6 says something similar. At Mount Sinai, God tells Israel that if they keep his *covenant*, they will be his treasure among all peoples. They will be a *kingdom of priests* and a holy nation. A priest serves God for others. Many readers think this means Israel was to show God to the nations.

Many readers connect these verses. Israel was God's portion, but not to keep God to itself. Christian readers often say Israel was meant to show the nations what God is like. Jewish readers also see Israel's calling as holy and lasting. Many stress living by God's teaching, the *Torah*, as the heart of that calling.

words.d: a binding agreement; in the Hebrew Bible, the bond between God and Israel
Exodus 19:6's name for Israel: a people who serve God on behalf of others
God's teaching; also the name for the first five books of the Bible

look.title: A Share of Land
look.text: Picture a farmer who divides his fields among his children. Each child gets a portion. But the farmer keeps one small field for himself. He plants it with care. Deuteronomy 32:8–9 uses this kind of picture. The nations get lands, and the LORD keeps Israel as his own portion.
look.prompt: In the picture, why might the farmer keep a field for himself? How does the picture help you read Deuteronomy 32:9?

check.q: Who is Jacob in Deuteronomy 32:9?
choices: Another name for Israel, God's people
One of the builders of Babel
check.why: Jacob, Abram's grandson, was also called Israel, so Jacob stands for the people of Israel in this verse.

check.q: What does Exodus 19:6 call Israel?
choices: A kingdom of priests and a holy nation
check.why: At Mount Sinai, Exodus 19:6 calls Israel a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.

check.q: What is the Torah?
choices: God's teaching; also the first five books of the Bible
check.why: Torah means God's teaching. It is also the name for the first five books of the Bible.

lessons.title: Rise Up, O God
lessons.mainIdea: Psalm 82:8 asks God to rise up and judge the earth because he will inherit all the nations.
reading: Psalm 82 begins with God standing in his council. He judges the elohim, the gods, because they do not defend the weak, the poor and the orphan. In verse 6 he calls them sons of the Most High. In verse 7 he says they will die like humans. Then comes verse 8.

In verse 8, the writer turns to God. He asks God to rise up and judge the earth. He gives a reason: God will *inherit* all the nations. In Hebrew, inherit comes from the same root as the inheritance in Deuteronomy 32:8. The two verses use the same word family.

Many scholars read Psalm 82 as a scene in God's heavenly council. E. Theodore Mullen (1980) and Mark S. Smith (2001) studied it beside the Ugarit tablets. Heiser read it as the answer to Babel. God judges the gods who ruled the nations badly, then takes the nations back. Other readers think the gods are human judges. For them, verse 8 asks God to set *justice* right.

words.d: to receive something as your own to keep, often from a parent
fair and right treatment for everyone, especially the weak

look.title: Psalm 82:8 in Simple Words
look.text: Rise up, O God, and judge the earth. For all the nations will belong to you.
look.cite: Psalm 82:8, paraphrased from the American Standard Version (1901)
look.prompt: Why does the writer ask God to judge the earth? How does the idea of inheriting connect back to Deuteronomy 32:8?

check.q: In Psalm 82, why does God judge the elohim?
choices: They built the tower of Babel
They did not defend the weak and the poor
check.why: Psalm 82 says God judges the elohim because they do not defend the weak, the poor and the orphan.

check.q: What does Psalm 82:8 say God will inherit?
check.why: Psalm 82:8 asks God to rise up, because he will inherit all the nations.

check.q: How do some other readers understand the gods in Psalm 82?
choices: As human judges who acted unfairly
As the seventy sons of El
check.why: Some Jewish and Christian readers take the gods of Psalm 82 to be human judges, not spirit beings.

lessons.title: A Light to the Nations
lessons.mainIdea: Isaiah 49:6 pictures God's servant as a light to the nations, so that God's rescue reaches the end of the earth.
reading: The book of Isaiah picks up the promise to Abram. In Isaiah 49:6, God speaks to his *servant*. It is too small a thing, God says, only to bring back the tribes of Jacob. God will also make the servant a light to the nations. Then his *salvation* will reach the end of the earth.

Readers differ on who the servant is. Many Jewish readers see the servant as Israel itself, as Isaiah 49:3 says. Some see a prophet. Christian readers have often seen the servant as pointing to Jesus. The New Testament quotes this verse in Acts 13:47. There Paul and Barnabas use it to describe their own work.

Isaiah 42:6 uses the same picture. There God gives his servant as a covenant for the people and a light for the nations. Many readers see a thread here that starts in Genesis 12. Abram's family was chosen, but not for itself alone. In this reading, the light was meant to spread to every nation.

words.d: someone who serves; in Isaiah, the one God sends to do his work
being rescued or kept safe; in Isaiah, God's rescue reaching people

look.title: Tracing a Thread
look.text: Genesis 12:3: all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abram. Isaiah 49:6: God's servant will be a light to the nations. Psalm 82:8: God will inherit all the nations.
look.prompt: What idea do these three verses share? Which words in each one show it?

check.q: What does Isaiah 49:6 say God's servant will be?
check.why: Isaiah 49:6 says God will make his servant a light to the nations.

check.q: Who do many Jewish readers think the servant is?
choices: One of the sons of God
check.why: Many Jewish readers see the servant as Israel, since Isaiah 49:3 calls the servant Israel.

check.q: Where does the New Testament quote Isaiah 49:6?
check.why: In Acts 13:47, Paul and Barnabas quote Isaiah 49:6 to describe their own work.

lessons.title: Jewish Readings of the Covenant
lessons.mainIdea: Jewish tradition honors Abraham as the father of the covenant people and tells how he turned from idols to the one God.
reading: In Genesis 15, God makes a covenant with Abram. He tells him to look at the stars and count them, if he can. So many, God says, will your offspring be. Genesis 15:6 says Abram believed the LORD. In Genesis 17, God changes his name to Abraham and gives the sign of the covenant.

Jewish tradition honors Abraham as the first father of the Jewish people. The covenant with him is seen as lasting. Many Jewish readers stress that it is lived out by keeping God's commandments, the *mitzvot*. The historian Josephus wrote that Abraham was the first to teach boldly that there is one God, the maker of all (Antiquities 1.7).

A famous old story, called a *midrash*, is told in Genesis Rabbah, a Jewish book on Genesis. In it, Abram's father Terah sold idols. Young Abram broke them and said the biggest idol did it. His father said idols cannot move. Abram asked, then why worship them? The story shows Abraham turning to the one God.

words.d: a Jewish way of explaining the Bible, often with stories; also a book of such teachings
the commandments in the Torah; one commandment is a mitzvah

look.title: Count the Stars
look.text: Genesis 15:5 pictures God taking Abram outside at night. God tells him to look up at the sky and count the stars, if he can. So many will your offspring be, God says. Abram has no children yet.
look.prompt: Why do you think the story uses the stars for this promise? How might Abram have felt, looking up?

check.q: In Genesis 15:5, what does God tell Abram to count?
check.why: Genesis 15:5 tells Abram to count the stars, if he can, because his offspring will be that many.

check.q: What is a midrash?
choices: A Greek translation of the Bible
A Jewish way of explaining the Bible, often with stories
check.why: A midrash is a Jewish way of explaining the Bible, often by telling a story, like the one in Genesis Rabbah.

check.q: In the midrash in Genesis Rabbah, what did young Abram do?
check.why: In the Genesis Rabbah story, Abram breaks his father's idols to show that idols cannot act.

lessons.title: Christian Readings: The Promise and Jesus
lessons.mainIdea: Paul wrote that the promise to Abraham was good news for the nations, and many Christians see Pentecost as Babel turned around.
reading: Christian readers have long read Genesis 12:3 as pointing to Jesus. In Galatians 3:8, Paul says the Scripture told the good news to Abraham ahead of time. He repeats the promise that all nations would be blessed in him. Paul taught that people from every nation could join Abraham's family through faith in Jesus (Galatians 3:29).

At the end of Matthew's Gospel, Jesus sends his followers to make *disciples* of all nations (Matthew 28:19). In Acts 2, at *Pentecost*, people from many lands hear the message in their own languages. Many Christian readers, Heiser among them, see this as Babel turned around. At Babel, languages split people apart. At Pentecost, one message came through many languages.

Jewish tradition links this festival, called Shavuot, to the giving of the Torah at Sinai. A teaching in the Talmud (Shabbat 88b) says each word God spoke there split into seventy languages. Jewish readers see the covenant with Abraham going on with the Jewish people, not pointing to Jesus. This course describes both readings without choosing between them.

words.d: students or followers of a teacher
a Jewish harvest festival; in Acts 2, the day Jesus' followers spoke in many languages

look.title: Galatians 3:8 in Simple Words
look.text: The Scripture saw ahead of time that God would make the nations right with him by faith. So it told the good news to Abraham early, saying: In you all the nations will be blessed.
look.cite: Galatians 3:8, paraphrased from the World English Bible
look.prompt: Which verse from Genesis 12 is Paul repeating? What does Paul say that verse announced?

check.q: In Galatians 3:8, what does Paul say was told to Abraham?
choices: The good news, ahead of time
check.why: Galatians 3:8 says the Scripture told the good news to Abraham ahead of time, repeating Genesis 12:3.

check.q: Why do many Christian readers see Pentecost as Babel turned around?
choices: Because at Babel languages split people, but at Pentecost one message came through many languages
Because Abram went back to Ur
Because the nations got new gods
check.why: At Babel, mixed-up languages scattered people. In Acts 2, people from many lands heard one message in their own languages.

check.q: In Matthew 28:19, where does Jesus send his followers?
check.why: Matthew 28:19 says Jesus sends his followers to make disciples of all nations.

review.q: Which town did Abram leave when he was seventy-five?
review.why: Genesis 12:4 says Abram was seventy-five when he left Haran.

review.q: Which promise in Genesis 12:3 reaches beyond Abram's own family?
choices: He will build a great city
All the families of the earth will be blessed through him
review.why: Genesis 12:3 promises that all the families of the earth will be blessed through Abram.

choices: God promises to make Abram's name great, instead of people making their own name
God sends Abram back to Babel
review.why: At Babel people tried to make a name for themselves. In Genesis 12:2 God promises Abram a great name.

review.q: What did Heiser think God was doing when he called Abram?
choices: Starting a new family to win back the nations
review.why: Heiser read Abram's call as God starting a new family through whom the nations would be won back.
Deuteronomy 32:9 says the LORD's portion is his people, Jacob, that is, Israel.

review.q: What does Psalm 82:8 ask God to do?
choices: Rise up and judge the earth, for he will inherit all the nations
review.why: Psalm 82:8 asks God to rise up and judge the earth, because he will inherit all the nations.

review.q: How do many Jewish readers see the covenant with Abraham?
choices: As only about the city of Ur
As lasting, lived out by the Jewish people through the commandments
review.why: Jewish tradition sees the covenant as lasting, passed down to Jewish families and lived out through the mitzvot.

review.q: What does a Talmud teaching (Shabbat 88b) say about God's words at Sinai?
choices: They were spoken only in Greek
They were written on a tower
review.why: Shabbat 88b says each word God spoke at Sinai split into seventy languages, one for each nation.
